items.prompt: A user requests "add a CSV export button." What's the key risk of building exactly that, without further investigation?
choices: CSV export is technically difficult to implement correctly
The request already encodes the requester's own assumed solution — building it literally means inheriting whatever unvalidated problem statement they had in mind, without confirming it's the best fit
Users never actually use export features once built
There is no risk; taking feature requests literally is always correct
items.explanation: A request phrased as a solution smuggles in an implicit, unvalidated problem statement. The risk isn't that CSV export is hard to build — it's that it might not actually be the best (or even a good) fit for the real underlying need, which was never separately checked.

items.prompt: Which of these passes the "one-sentence problem statement" test from L2 (states the problem with zero reference to the proposed solution)?
choices: "Users need a CSV export so they can track trends"
"Users need to notice when a metric is trending in the wrong direction, in time to act, without a manual weekly ritual"
"Users want a dark mode toggle"
"We should add bulk delete for tickets"
items.explanation: The first, third, and fourth options each bake a specific solution into the problem statement itself, which forecloses comparing alternatives. Only the second describes the underlying need without naming how it should be solved.

items.prompt: "I want a CSV export so I can build a report." Per L3's failure modes, is this a good stopping point for the five-whys process?
choices: Yes — "so I can build a report" is clearly a root need
No — "a report" is itself still a solution-shaped answer, not a root need; the technique's value comes from pushing past the first plausible-sounding answer
Yes, because any answer after the first "why" counts as sufficient
No, because five whys always requires exactly five iterations, no more, no less
items.explanation: Stopping at the first answer and calling it the root need is one of L3's explicit failure modes — a report is a chosen solution too, just one step removed from CSV export. The technique needs to be pushed until the answer is genuinely a need, not another solution wearing different clothes.

items.prompt: Two users both ask for "a way to see this metric over time." One needs it for a quick weekly glance; the other needs it for a one-off deep investigation. Per the "jobs to be done" framing, why does this context matter?
choices: It doesn't — the same feature (a chart) always serves both cases equally well

The same underlying need calls for different solutions depending on context — a lightweight recurring glance and a deep one-time analysis are different jobs, even though both are nominally "see this metric over time"
Context only matters for enterprise customers, not general users
Jobs to be done applies only to entirely new products, not existing features
items.explanation: Jobs to be done frames a need as tied to a specific context, not just an abstract description. A generic CSV export serves a deep one-off investigation reasonably well but poorly serves a routine quick glance — the same words ("see trends") hide two different jobs with different best-fit solutions.

items.prompt: In L3's dark mode case, three users request the same feature for different underlying reasons (eye strain, visual parity, aesthetic preference). What did treating them as "the same request" risk, if the team hadn't separated the whys per requester?
choices: Nothing — since they all requested the same feature, the underlying reason is irrelevant to shipping it

Missing that one requester's need (eye strain) correlated with a real usability pattern worth prioritizing urgently, which got surfaced specifically because the whys were traced per-requester rather than assumed to be identical
Building three separate dark mode features, one per user segment
The five whys process cannot be applied when multiple users request the same feature
items.explanation: A literal reading treats all three requesters as wanting the identical thing for the identical reason. Tracing the whys separately revealed genuinely different weights behind an outwardly identical request — information that directly informed prioritization (urgent usability pain vs. pure preference), which would have been invisible if the team had stopped at "they all want dark mode."

items.prompt: Per L3's last failure mode, should every feature request go through a full five-whys investigation before any work starts?
choices: Yes, always — skipping it for any request risks building the wrong thing

No — the depth of investigation should be proportional to the cost and risk of the requested solution; a one-hour UI tweak doesn't warrant the same scrutiny as a destructive, hard-to-reverse feature like bulk delete
No — the five whys should only ever be used for entirely new products, never existing features
Yes, but only for requests that come from more than one user
items.explanation: L3 explicitly warns against applying this so rigorously that trivial, cheap requests get needlessly interrogated — the value of validating the problem has to be weighed against the cost of the investigation itself, scaled to how risky or expensive the proposed solution actually is.
